item.title: Latino Voters Reshape Electoral Map Once Again
item.description:
Latino voters transformed American politics Tuesday night — yet again.

In Texas and Kansas, Colorado and California, Latinos voted for Democrats in huge numbers, helping determine control of both the House and Senate just two years after they had flocked to Republicans and propelled Donald Trump back to the White House.

Hispanic lawmakers will make up roughly a fifth of the Democratic majority in the House, a record. And for the first time in modern history, California and Texas, the two largest states in the country, will be led by Latino governors — both Democrats.

It was an unraveling of the multiracial coalition that Republicans celebrated in 2024. Just last year, Republicans were so confident that their gains with Hispanic voters promised a new era that they gerrymandered five districts in Texas with the assumption that those voters would remain on their side. On Tuesday, Democrats ended up winning four of those seats.

For years, Latino voters have complained about being ignored by politicians in both parties. Now, they have the attention of Republicans and Democrats, playing a role that could shape government policy especially on the economy and immigration.

Note: Shift is a comparison to the 2024 presidential margin in districts that have reported almost all of their votes. Where district boundaries were changed, 2024 presidential results were reapportioned to new district shapes.

“You can draw the lines, but you can’t predict Latino voters,” said Erica Bernal-Martinez, the chief executive officer of the National Association of Latino Elected Officials, a nonpartisan group. “Latinos sent a message every party, campaign and mapmaker needs to hear: Our vote cannot be assumed, and it will never be taken for granted.”

As Democrats ran up huge margins all over the country, their support from Hispanic voters was one of the most important demographic shifts. In 2024, Republicans received roughly 44 percent of the Latino vote. On Tuesday, the G.O.P.’s share had shrunk back to 30 percent, slightly higher than the historic average.

But there were clear reminders that the group remains far from monolithic. In conservative strongholds in Florida, Republicans appeared poised to hold onto their seats in majority-Latino districts, though with far narrower margins than in recent years.

Representative Maria Elvira Salazar, who has represented Miami for three terms, enraged her fellow Republicans when she released an ad in October warning that the party would lose Hispanic voters because of the Trump administration’s aggressive immigration enforcement tactics. But the results Tuesday night suggested she was right.

At her party in Miami, she told supporters that it was a “moment of reckoning.”

“I am here to help the Republican Party and the White House understand what my community is saying loud and clear,” she said, adding that Hispanic voters want “want a secure border, but they also want an immigration system that respects the dignity of hard-working people.”

On Wednesday evening, votes were still being counted in Ms. Salazar’s district.

While Senator Ashley Moody, a Republican, was re-elected in Florida, results showed that Hispanic voters supported the Democratic challenger, Angie Nixon, by a significantly greater margin than they had backed the Democrat in 2024.

Shift in margin

Majority Hispanic counties

Note: Shift is a comparison to the 2024 presidential margin in counties that have reported almost all of their votes.

The Latino shift away from Republicans could not be blamed on immigration policy alone.

Latino voters also revolted for many of the same reasons they chose President Trump in the first place: They were furious about the cost of living and believed politicians in power were ignoring their struggles. For some Latinos, the issues of immigration and the economy are inextricably linked. Many live in areas that depend on immigrant labor and have seen the local economy plummet amid deportations. The shift among Hispanic voters was a mirror image of 2024: It happened all over the country, in urban and rural districts, with women and men. Hispanic voters without college degrees showed the most significant shift, moving 33 points toward Democrats.

Republican gains two years ago also relied heavily on young voters, and those too were largely wiped out, driven by Hispanic voters who skew younger than white voters. Roughly two in three Hispanic voters are under the age of 50, compared with less than half of white voters.

The swing was among the most decisive in Texas, where Latinos make up roughly a quarter of all voters, and their support for Republicans was pared back significantly. Democrats won all along the southern border in majority Hispanic counties, fulfilling their long-promised dreams of a blue Texas.

In Webb and Hidalgo, two Hispanic-majority counties where Democrats easily won for decades, voters delivered a shocking victory for Republicans in 2024, but favored the Democratic Senate candidate, James Talarico, by roughly 50 points on Tuesday.

Shift in margin

Majority Hispanic counties

Note: Shift is a comparison to the 2024 presidential margin in counties that have reported almost all of their votes.

Few candidates captured the imagination of Hispanic voters in Texas like Bobby Pulido, a Latin Grammy Award-winning Tejano singer who campaigned for the House at dozens of quinceañeras throughout his district. With supporters decked in rhinestone cowboy boots, his election night celebration took on the atmosphere of the kind of parties he said were crucial to winning the race.

“People are tired of one-party rule, and they want us to work together and they want results,” he said. “People cannot be used as a political football anymore.”

As he took the stage, a group of young mariachi players watched with tears in their eyes. Earlier this year, two members of the group were held in federal immigration detention. The family had entered the United States through the Brownsville border crossing on an asylum claim and their case drew national outrage, becoming a campaign issue in the race between Mr. Pulido, a Democrat, and Representative Monica De La Cruz, the Republican incumbent who had hosted the musicians in Washington. After their release, the group performed at several events for Mr. Pulido.

“I’m just so happy and relieved,” said Lea Garcia, 20, wearing the group’s signature gold velvet mariachi suit. “I just want to be able buy a house, to get married and to have kids and stay in this state I love. And I want my friends to be able to stay here.

Mr. Pulido said he would make overhauling the country’s broken immigration system a top priority in Washington.

In California, the shift was slightly more modest, with roughly three-quarters of Latino voters in the state backing Democrats in the House, a shift of 29 percentage points from 2024. That was enough to flip the 22nd Congressional District, which snakes through the Central Valley and has long been one of the most important targets for Democrats in the state. Latinos make up roughly 64 percent of the district and fueled the election of Randy Villegas, a progressive community college professor who will become the first Latino to represent the district.

In Kansas, two Hispanic-majority counties in the rural western area of the state, Finney and Seward, shifted roughly 50 percentage points to Democrats. The area is home to a large number of meatpacking plants and is known as the golden triangle of beef. Immigration officials carried out several raids in the region this fall.

While Democratic wins were significant in Hispanic-majority areas, the shifts were not limited there. Even in districts that are not majority-Hispanic but where many political strategists saw Latino voters as pivotal, Democrats won in nearly every single contest.

Democrats also secured crucial victories in Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Pennsylvania, in congressional districts with sizable Latino populations that had swung toward Republicans in 2024.

In the New Mexico Senate race, majority-Hispanic counties shifted toward the Democratic candidate by a significant margin, compared with 2024.

Shift in margin

Majority Hispanic counties

Note: Shift is a comparison to the 2024 presidential margin in counties that have reported almost all of their votes.

There is little to suggest that this year’s swing signals a steadfast loyalty to Democrats among Hispanic voters.

“The G.O.P. paid the price for being the party in power and not delivering,” said Daniel Garza, the executive director of Libre, a conservative group that works to persuade Latinos to vote for Republicans. “What’s at play is the middle, the voters that are swinging wildly. They have no home. There is no loyalty if they feel they are being ignored.”

In the Rio Grande Valley, Ms. De La Cruz had become the first Republican in modern history to represent the district when she was elected in 2022. Along with other conservative Latinas in South Texas and Florida, she was widely hailed as a new star in the party. But her rise ended as suddenly as it began.

At the party for Ms. De La Cruz Tuesday, the campaign distributed white baseball hats embroidered with “Puro 956,” a nod to the local area code. Two hours after the polls closed, she emerged to concede to Mr. Pulido. Her speech lasted less than two minutes.

“I want to thank all the people who have worked so hard over the last week because you believed in me,” she said after acknowledging her defeat. “You believed in South Texas and you believed in this country.”

Ruth Igielnik and Rylan Renteria contributed reporting.

]]>

item.title: How Texas Democrats Turned Decades of Defeat Into a Statewide Sweep
item.description:
The Democratic Party’s stunning domination in Texas on Tuesday began with the promise of one candidate, James Talarico.

After decades of Republican rule, his well-funded, disciplined and scandal-free U.S. Senate campaign helped convince voters that winning was possible this time. He soon had help.

Gina Hinojosa, a little-known state lawmaker who had appeared destined for defeat when she challenged Gov. Greg Abbott, emphasized the issue of data centers, sitting in the living rooms of conservatives angry about the massive, noisy, energy-guzzling facilities. She promised a halt.

Behind them both was the deepest bench of Democratic candidates assembled in decades in Texas. Transcending any single person, the party built quiet momentum with voters fed up with rising prices and unmoved by Republican warnings that voting for Democrats would signal the end of Texas as they knew it.

With Democrats poised to occupy nearly every statewide office — a tectonic shift — top campaign advisers, newly elected leaders, party operatives and strategists described in interviews how Mr. Talarico’s campaign had galvanized voters and fueled improbable triumphs.

They also credited a yearslong organizing effort and the party’s success at fielding candidates for nearly every race — all 150 state House districts, every statewide office, every state board of education position and every major judicial race. The Republican Party in Texas did not do the same, leaving some Democrats with uncontested seats.

“This is the first year where we really had a machine built,” said Katherine Fischer, the executive director of the Texas Majority PAC, which worked with the Texas Democratic Party to run and train candidates. “We filled every single state and federal seat for the first time in state history of either party.”

By Wednesday, the scale of Democratic success was so great that it appeared likely to propel a legislative candidate in Fort Worth’s conservative suburbs to victory despite having suspended her campaign over questions about whether a conviction could disqualify her.

The results surprised even winning candidates, who were in a state of elated shock on Tuesday night.

“I had no idea what was going to happen. Frankly, none of us did,” said Sarah Eckhardt, the comptroller-elect, as she stood in a Whataburger restaurant in Austin packed with jubilant Democrats.

Mr. Talarico and Ms. Hinojosa, who will be the state’s first Latina governor, sat at a table and toasted with orange-and-white soda cups as giddy supporters cheered and snapped photos.

“We’re in a realignment that goes beyond party,” Ms. Eckhardt added. “That’s what’s happening here.”

Republican Party leaders had long assumed that the only threats to their power were from the right, even as Texas became a landing pad for transplants and immigrants, its cosmopolitan urban centers ballooning to include five of the nation’s 15 largest cities.

That assumption that moving right was always the right move led Ken Paxton, a scandal-scarred attorney general, to challenge and defeat Senator John Cornyn in the primary. It also allowed Bo French, a brazenly anti-Muslim candidate, to become the party’s nominee for oil and gas regulator. He complained publicly about the number of South Asians at the University of Texas. He lost.

The long rightward lurch had not been a problem for Republican officials. Then, on Tuesday, the lurch back swept most of them away.

The Democratic Party’s candidates, especially in statewide races, stuck to a consistent middle-of-the-road message, promising to address cost-of-living concerns and to curtail cultural battles that have consumed Texas politics for years.

For many, including Ms. Hinojosa, the biggest challenge was being taken seriously, especially by major donors.

“It was really hard to get people to believe in this race,” said Amy Friedman, her campaign manager. “It was a slog to get our first million. It was a slog to get the next two.”

By contrast, Republicans leaned into culture wars that had seemed potent just two years before. They believed they had easy targets in Ms. Hinojosa and Mr. Talarico, who had spoken publicly about gender, race and equity.

“Some people know him as ‘Tofu Talarico.’ Some people call him ‘Six Gender Jimmy,’” said Mr. Paxton on the night of his primary victory in March. “I’ve even heard some people even call him James Talafreako.”

That nickname stuck, but not as Mr. Paxton expected.t

At a Houston rally the next day, Mr. Talarico told supporters that they could buy a T-shirt declaring “I’m a Talafreako.” More than 43,000 did, netting his campaign more than $1 million.

The nimble response — parrying rather than counterpunching — captured the instincts of his campaign. Mr. Talarico stuck relentlessly to a core message: Texas politics was dominated by billionaires and politicians like Mr. Paxton who had served their own interests at the expense of ordinary Texans.

Mr. Talarico navigated fraught moments in his speeches, often germinating in iPhone notes shared with his 26-year-old speechwriter, Antonio Esparza.

On Sept. 10, 2025, the day after Mr. Talarico announced his Senate run, he learned that Charlie Kirk, the conservative activist, had been assassinated. He was at his Austin home with Mr. Esparza when they decided to directly address the killing at a planned rally that night, “instead of running from it,” Mr. Esparza said.

They wrote a speech as they drove to a San Antonio rally in Mr. Talarico’s pickup, driven by another aide, each on his own laptop in a shared document, typing as they headed down Interstate 35.

“I disagreed with Charlie Kirk on almost every political issue, but Charlie Kirk was a child of God,” Mr. Talarico, a former seminarian, said in the speech. “He was our sibling, our brother. He was a human being.”

A video of the remarks, clipped and shared on social media, spread widely.

“I’ll never forget being in that truck,” Mr. Esparza said.

The approach underscored what Mr. Talarico presented in his campaign as a commitment to bipartisanship, to faith and to getting beyond divisions. He hammered home that message to audiences listening to hourlong podcasts. He delivered it in person around the state, first with town halls where he took questions and then in speeches to thousands.

The message of ending division and transcending partisanship united the ticket in 2026. It was repeated by candidates like Taylor Rehmet, a union machinist uncomfortable with party labels, who flipped a State Senate seat in a deep-red district in Tarrant County in a January special election and held onto the seat on Tuesday. It was also part of Ms. Hinojosa’s victory speech in Austin.

“Whether you’re a Democrat, a Republican or neither,” Ms. Hinojosa said, “hear what Texas said today, loud and clear: Your government belongs to you.”

Ms. Hinojosa at first struggled to gain attention, but she often met with individual voters, and spent time trying to understand issues like data centers before becoming among the most prominent Texas politicians to support a moratorium.

“We had months of meetings before that rollout,” said Ms. Friedman, the campaign manager. Ms. Hinojosa wanted to talk to people directly affected and to know where labor organizations stood.

Democrats also had to regain support from Latino voters. They did so by not taking it for granted, said Regina Montoya, a board member of the Latino Victory Fund political action committee. She recalled Mr. Talarico visiting her at home in Dallas last year as he embarked on his campaign. They shared breakfast tacos.

“He was there to listen,” Ms. Montoya said. “He promised then that he would work hard to earn the votes of Latinos.”

Mr. Talarico accomplished that also through deft use of social media, courting influencers while he was running in a tough Democratic primary.

“His skill is being genuine, and this is not like an ideology thing. It’s like a personality thing,” said Carlos Espina, a Texas-based progressive influencer who makes videos in Spanish. Mr. Espina, who has said he was not paid by the campaign for his videos backing Mr. Talarico, also said the bipartisan message resonated with Latinos.

“We don’t say, ‘Oh, it’s Democrat and Republican,’” he said. “This is a right or wrong thing. Like, should you be treating people this way as human beings?”

The Democrats at the top of the ticket also magnified each other through joint appearances, introducing one another to new audiences. Mr. Talarico teamed up for events with Ms. Hinojosa and with Bobby Pulido, a well-known Tejano singer who flipped a congressional district in the Rio Grande Valley on Tuesday.

And Democrats also had one major, if unintentional, benefactor: President Trump, who visited the state repeatedly, reminding voters of why he was unpopular.

“The biggest thanks have to go to Donald Trump,” said Cristóbal Alex, who helped advise a super PAC supporting Mr. Talarico.

He said the president’s endorsement of Mr. Paxton could have made them a powerful Republican force. Instead, he said, it backfired.

“It’s like the two of them are part of this political A team,” Mr. Alex said. “Except the A team was the C team.”

item.title: ‘Florida Is the Last Main Anchor Standing’ for Republicans
item.description:
On a midterm election night awash in blue, one significant corner of the country stayed red.

Florida, the third most populous state, withstood a national Democratic surge on Tuesday, remaining a Republican bastion even as the G.O.P. amassed deep losses in Texas and across the electoral map.

“We got wiped out in Texas, the biggest anchor we have in Republican politics,” Gov. Ron DeSantis of Florida said on Wednesday. “So really, Florida is the last main anchor standing.”

Florida Republicans held onto a U.S. Senate seat, the governor’s mansion and every statewide office. Those victories were a point of pride for the national party on a night with few celebratory moments, especially in the South. They appeared to reinforce Florida’s standing as a former battleground state that is now solidly Republican.

But even in Florida, Republicans lost some of their oomph.

The party will no longer enjoy supermajorities in the State Legislature, with Democrats netting at least 15 seats, more than they had in decades. Democrats were also on track to retain eight of the state’s 28 congressional seats, the same number they had before the midterms, even after Republican state lawmakers redrew four districts in their favor this spring.

Democrats flipped Miami-Dade County, which Republicans had boasted about winning in 2022 and 2024. And Republican candidates only narrowly won the races for Senate and governor despite vast advantages in fund-raising and voter registration, giving the party a scare.

Senator Ashley Moody, the Republican incumbent, defeated Angie Nixon, her Democratic challenger, by about three percentage points. Byron Donalds, the Republican governor-elect, edged out David Jolly, the Democratic nominee, by about one percentage point — or about 108,000 votes out of more than 8.2 million cast. Mr. Donalds outspent Mr. Jolly by about $150 million.

In contrast, in 2022, Mr. DeSantis, who is term limited, won re-election by nearly 20 points and Senator Marco Rubio by 16 percentage points. Two years ago, President Trump won his adopted home state by 13 percentage points.

“It has been the honor of a lifetime to move this state 14 points in a new direction,” Mr. Jolly said in an emotional concession speech in Tampa on Tuesday night. “Somewhere out there tonight is someone that in the next cycle is going to get it across the finish line.”

For Florida Democrats, the close results were evidence that the national party and its donors, who abandoned the state during the DeSantis era, should invest again. Florida’s size and 10 television markets make campaigning very expensive, though Mr. Jolly and especially Ms. Nixon — who ran a grass-roots operation with no television ads — showed how far limited resources could go.

“Florida Democrats are looking at the results across the country and can only imagine what kind of day we would be having if we had sustained national support,” Nikki Fried, the Florida Democratic Party chairwoman, told reporters on Wednesday.

Still, Florida Democrats could not win statewide races in a year that saw a generational shift in the party’s favor nationally. They also fell just short of winning races for Senate and governor in 2018, another blue-wave midterm.

On Tuesday, their biggest obstacle may have been the enormous lead that Republicans have in voter registration, said Matthew Isbell, a Democratic elections data analyst in the state. National Democrats could have invested in voter registration efforts a year ago, he said, to capitalize on the deep voter discontent with Mr. Trump and his party.

“It was a missed opportunity — this could have been won,” Mr. Isbell said. “If we have the resources, we could start to tilt Florida back to a purplish state, or at least light red.”

As he finishes his eighth year in office, Mr. DeSantis, a proud and pugnacious culture warrior whose “war on woke” raised his national profile, remains the most popular Republican in the state. He did not endorse Mr. Donalds or any other Republican in the primary to succeed him. And he made only a few campaign appearances ahead of the general election, perhaps knowing that Mr. Trump’s unpopularity had hamstrung Republican candidates. (Mr. DeSantis lost to Mr. Trump in the 2024 presidential primary.)

Especially since the coronavirus pandemic, Mr. DeSantis has governed by pushing the limits of his executive power and muscling through his conservative priorities — even if they appeared far to the political right of many Floridians. He has argued that such an aggressive approach has grown the state Republican Party by drawing new residents and winning over existing ones who want their elected leaders to stand for something.

At a news conference on Wednesday, he called the national midterm results “as close to an extinction-level event for Republicans in many parts of the country as we have seen probably in the last 100 years.”

“I don’t think most of us thought it would be this bad,” Mr. DeSantis said.

Some Florida voters may have been motivated to turn out for a ballot measure, known as Amendment 3, that would dramatically cut property taxes on primary homes. The measure, which passed with about 62 percent support, has divided Republican leaders. It is expected to cost local governments billions of dollars in revenue and lead to sharp reductions in public services or to new local fees or taxes — all of which could complicate governing for Mr. Donalds.

“Byron Donalds is about to be handed a dumpster fire of problems, and we are running a live experiment on 23 million Floridians,” said Jeff Brandes, a former Republican state senator and president of the Florida Policy Project, a think tank.

None of that was top of mind as Mr. Donalds took the stage in Hollywood, Fla., on Tuesday night to celebrate keeping the governorship in Republican hands since 1999, when Gov. Jeb Bush took office.

“Mr. President, I want you to hear from Florida,” he said, addressing Mr. Trump. “We are still red.”

Alan Blinder contributed reporting from Tampa, Fla.
